questions.title: Define AI
questions.text: Define the term **artificial intelligence**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The ability of a computer / machine to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence (1)
- e.g. learning, reasoning, problem solving, recognising speech / images, making decisions (1)

points.criterion: Machine performing tasks needing human intelligence

scheme.model_answer: The ability of a computer system to carry out tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech, making decisions and learning from experience.

questions.title: AI, ML and DL
questions.text: Which statement about AI, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) is correct?

options.content: AI is a subset of deep learning
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
Machine learning and AI are unrelated
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: The fields are nested: DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI.

questions.title: Match the definitions
questions.text: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Machines performing tasks that normally need human intelligence
Systems that learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed
Learning with neural networks that have many hidden layers

scheme.mark_scheme: AI–R1, ML–R2, DL–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Define machine learning
questions.text: Define **machine learning**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A branch / subset of AI in which the computer learns from data / examples (1)
- to find patterns / make predictions and improve with experience without being explicitly programmed (1)
scheme.model_answer: A branch of AI in which a computer learns patterns from data and improves its predictions with experience, without being explicitly programmed with the rules.

questions.title: ML vs DL
questions.text: Identify **two** differences between machine learning and deep learning.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): DL uses neural networks with many hidden layers vs ML can use simpler models; DL needs much more data; DL needs much more computing power / GPUs; DL finds features automatically vs ML often needs humans to choose features; DL is harder to explain (black box); DL is a subset of ML
scheme.model_answer: 1 Deep learning uses neural networks with many hidden layers, whereas machine learning can use simpler models. 2 Deep learning needs far more data and computing power.

questions.title: AI vs ML
questions.text: An expert system that diagnoses car faults uses rules written by mechanics. Explain why it is an example of **AI** but **not** of machine learning.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- It is AI because it performs a task that needs human (expert) intelligence / makes decisions (1)
- It is not ML because its rules are written / programmed by people, it does not learn them from data (1)

points.criterion: Not ML: rules are programmed, not learnt from data

scheme.model_answer: It is AI because it makes decisions that would normally need an expert mechanic, but it is not machine learning because its rules were written by people rather than learnt from data.

questions.title: Types of machine learning
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of machine learning used.

prefill: Learning to recognise spam from e-mails labelled 'spam' or 'not spam'
Grouping customers by their buying habits without any labels
A robot learning to walk by receiving rewards when it does not fall

scheme.mark_scheme: Spam → Supervised (1); Customer groups → Unsupervised (1); Robot → Reinforcement (1)

questions.title: Neural networks
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

A neural network has an input layer, one or more [[1]] layers and an output layer. During training the [[2]] of the connections are adjusted to reduce the error. A network with many of these layers is used in [[3]] learning.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) hidden (2) weights (3) deep

questions.title: Data for deep learning
questions.text: Deep learning usually needs very large amounts of training data and a lot of computing power.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Deep networks have millions of weights, so they need large data sets and powerful hardware such as GPUs to train.

questions.title: How a spam filter learns
questions.text: Explain how a machine-learning spam filter learns to recognise spam e-mails.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three (1 each):
- It is given a large set of training e-mails labelled spam / not spam (supervised)
- It finds patterns / features common in spam (words, links, senders)
- It builds a model that predicts whether a new e-mail is spam
- Its predictions are compared with the correct labels / errors are used to adjust the model
- It improves as users mark more e-mails as spam / more data
scheme.model_answer: It is trained on thousands of e-mails labelled spam or not spam. It finds patterns that are common in spam, such as certain words and links, and builds a model that predicts whether a new e-mail is spam. When users mark mistakes, the model is adjusted, so it keeps improving.

questions.title: AI in different areas
questions.text: Give **one** example of the use of AI in each of the following areas.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Medicine (1): diagnosing diseases from scans; drug discovery; predicting patient risk; robotic surgery
Transport (1): self-driving cars; traffic control; route planning / traffic prediction; autopilot
Finance (1): fraud detection; credit scoring; algorithmic trading; banking chatbots
scheme.model_answer: Medicine: detecting cancer on X-ray images. Transport: self-driving cars. Finance: detecting fraudulent card payments.

questions.title: Advantages of AI
questions.text: Select **two** advantages of using AI in society.

options.content: It can work 24 hours a day without getting tired
It always makes fair decisions whatever data it was trained on
It can carry out dangerous tasks instead of humans

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: AI can be biased if its data is biased, and it often needs large amounts of personal data.

questions.title: Disadvantages of AI
questions.text: Identify **two** disadvantages of using artificial intelligence in society.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): job losses / unemployment; bias / unfair decisions; privacy / large amounts of personal data / surveillance; lack of transparency / black box; unclear responsibility / accountability; misuse — deepfakes, fake news, cyber-attacks, weapons; high cost / energy; over-reliance / loss of skills; no common sense / empathy
scheme.model_answer: 1 People doing routine jobs, such as cashiers, may lose their jobs. 2 An AI trained on biased data may make unfair decisions.

questions.title: Bias in AI
questions.text: A company uses an AI system to choose which job applicants to invite to interview. It was trained on the CVs of people the company hired in the past ten years. Explain why the system's decisions might be **unfair**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The AI learns patterns from past decisions / training data (1)
- If past hiring was biased (e.g. mostly men / one group), the AI copies the bias and rejects other groups / it is hard to see why it decided (1)

points.criterion: Past bias is repeated / unfair to some groups

scheme.model_answer: The AI learns from the company's past decisions. If in the past the company mostly hired one group of people, the AI will learn that pattern and unfairly reject good applicants from other groups.

questions.title: AI and jobs
questions.text: AI only removes jobs and never creates new ones.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: AI automates some routine jobs but also creates new ones, such as AI engineers, data scientists and technicians who maintain AI systems.

questions.title: VR vs AR
questions.text: Explain the difference between **virtual reality** and **augmented reality**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- VR replaces the user's view with a completely computer-generated environment / the real world is not seen (1)
- AR adds digital information / objects on top of the real-world view, which is still visible (1)

points.criterion: AR adds to the real world

scheme.model_answer: Virtual reality replaces the user's view with a completely computer-generated world, whereas augmented reality adds digital objects and information on top of the real world, which the user can still see.

questions.title: VR or AR
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether each application uses **virtual** or **augmented** reality.

prefill: A flight simulator headset for training pilots
A phone app that shows how a new sofa would look in your living room
A game in which creatures appear on the real street through the phone camera
A headset tour of the inside of a pyramid

scheme.mark_scheme: Flight simulator → VR (1); Sofa app → AR (1); Street game → AR (1); Pyramid tour → VR (1)

questions.title: Purpose of VR
questions.text: Explain the purpose of virtual reality in training **surgeons**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Surgeons can practise operations in a realistic, immersive simulated environment (1)
- without any risk to real patients / mistakes can be repeated and learned from / cheaper than real practice (1)

points.criterion: No risk to patients / can repeat

scheme.model_answer: VR lets surgeons practise operations in a realistic simulated operating theatre, so they can make and learn from mistakes without any risk to real patients.

questions.title: AI cameras in a city
questions.text:
A city plans to install AI cameras with face recognition on every street to find wanted criminals and missing people.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this plan for society.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantages (max 2): criminals / missing people found faster; works 24/7; analyses huge amounts of video humans could not; may deter crime / safer streets
Disadvantages (max 2): loss of privacy / mass surveillance of innocent people; false matches — innocent people stopped / bias against some groups; data could be hacked / misused by the government; expensive
A balanced answer with points linked to the scenario for 4.

points.criterion: First advantage linked to the scenario
First disadvantage linked to the scenario

scheme.model_answer: The cameras could find wanted criminals and missing children much faster than police watching videos, and they work 24 hours a day, which may make the streets safer. However, everyone's movements would be recorded, which is a serious loss of privacy for innocent people. The system can also make false matches, especially if it was trained on biased data, so innocent people might be stopped by the police.
scheme.ai_instructions: Maximum 2 if only advantages or only disadvantages are given.

questions.title: AI in a school
questions.text: A school introduces an AI learning platform that chooses each student's next exercise based on their previous answers, and uses AR apps in biology lessons.

parts.title: Why it is ML
parts.text: Explain why the learning platform is an example of **machine learning**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- It learns from data — the students' previous answers (1)
- to predict / choose suitable exercises and improves as it receives more answers, without the rules being programmed (1)
scheme.model_answer: It learns from data — each student's previous answers — and uses the patterns it finds to choose suitable exercises, improving as more answers are collected rather than following fixed programmed rules.

parts.title: Advantage and disadvantage
parts.text: Identify **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of the AI platform for students.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): personalised learning / own pace; instant feedback; available any time; focuses on weak areas
Disadvantage (1): personal data collected / privacy; less contact with teachers / no empathy; may make wrong choices / bias; over-reliance; needs devices / Internet
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: each student gets exercises at the right level for them. Disadvantage: a lot of personal data about each student is collected.

parts.title: AR in biology
parts.text: Explain the purpose of using augmented reality in biology lessons.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- AR adds 3D models / information to the real view, e.g. a beating heart appears on the desk / over a textbook (1)
- students can see and interact with structures that are hard to imagine / makes learning more engaging and easier to understand (1)

points.criterion: Adds 3D models / information to the real view

scheme.model_answer: When students point a tablet at the textbook, a 3D model of a beating heart appears on the page, so they can rotate it and understand its structure much more easily than from a flat picture.

questions.title: AI and society
questions.text: "Artificial intelligence will do more good than harm to society." Discuss this statement. Refer to **at least two** areas where AI is used.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantages with examples (max 3): faster / more accurate diagnosis in medicine; fewer accidents with self-driving cars; fraud detection; personalised education; dangerous / repetitive work done by robots; 24/7
Disadvantages with examples (max 3): job losses (drivers, cashiers); bias in hiring / loans; privacy / surveillance; deepfakes / misinformation; unclear accountability; black-box decisions
Conclusion (1) that weighs the points
[Max 6] — at least two areas must be referred to for full marks
scheme.model_answer: In medicine, AI can analyse X-rays faster and sometimes more accurately than doctors, so diseases are found earlier. In transport, self-driving cars could reduce accidents caused by tired or distracted drivers, and AI can do dangerous jobs in mines or factories. However, AI may replace drivers, cashiers and call-centre staff, causing unemployment. AI trained on biased data can make unfair decisions about loans or jobs, and face recognition threatens privacy. It is also unclear who is responsible when an AI makes a harmful mistake. Overall, AI can do more good than harm only if it is regulated, trained on fair data and its decisions are checked by people.

questions.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning
questions.text: Artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning are closely related.

parts.title: Definitions
parts.text: Draw a line to link each term to its description.

right.text: Uses neural networks with many layers to learn from very large data sets
The broad field of making machines perform tasks that need human intelligence
Learns patterns from data and improves with experience without being explicitly programmed

scheme.mark_scheme: AI–R2, ML–R3, DL–R1. One mark per correct line.

parts.title: ML vs DL
parts.text: Identify **two** differences between machine learning and deep learning.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): many-layered neural networks vs simpler models; much more data; much more computing power; features learnt automatically vs chosen by humans; harder to explain; DL is a subset of ML
scheme.model_answer: 1 Deep learning uses neural networks with many hidden layers. 2 Deep learning needs much larger amounts of data and computing power.

parts.title: How a system learns
parts.text: A phone app learns to recognise different types of flower from photos. Explain how a machine-learning system can learn to do this.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): trained on many photos labelled with the flower name; finds patterns / features (colour, shape of petals); builds a model / neural network that predicts the label of a new photo; errors compared with correct labels and weights adjusted; accuracy improves with more data / repeated training

points.criterion: Adjusts using errors / improves with data

scheme.model_answer: The system is trained on thousands of photos, each labelled with the name of the flower. It finds patterns such as petal shape and colour and builds a model that predicts the name for a new photo. Its wrong predictions are used to adjust the model, so it becomes more accurate with more training data.

questions.title: AI in society
questions.text: Artificial intelligence is used more and more in everyday life.

parts.title: Examples of AI
parts.text: Give **one** example of the use of AI in each area.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Medicine (1): disease diagnosis; medical image interpretation; drug discovery; personalised treatment
Education (1): adaptive learning platforms; automatic marking; AI tutors / chatbots; plagiarism detection
scheme.model_answer: Medicine: interpreting X-ray and MRI images. Education: a platform that adapts exercises to each student.

parts.title: Advantages
parts.text: Identify **two** advantages of using artificial intelligence in society.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): works 24/7; faster; fewer human errors / consistent; dangerous or repetitive tasks; analyses large amounts of data; personalised services; helps people with disabilities; creates new jobs
scheme.model_answer: 1 It can do dangerous jobs, such as inspecting nuclear reactors, instead of people. 2 It can work 24 hours a day without getting tired.

parts.title: Disadvantages explained
parts.text: Explain **two** disadvantages of using artificial intelligence in society.

scheme.mark_scheme:
For each of two disadvantages: disadvantage (1) + explanation (1), e.g.
- Job losses (1): routine jobs such as drivers / cashiers are automated, causing unemployment (1)
- Bias (1): trained on biased data, so unfair decisions about loans / jobs (1)
- Privacy (1): needs large amounts of personal data / surveillance (1)
- Accountability (1): unclear who is responsible when AI makes a harmful mistake (1)
- Misuse (1): deepfakes / fake news can deceive people (1)
scheme.model_answer: AI can automate routine jobs such as driving taxis or working at a till, so many people may become unemployed. AI also needs huge amounts of personal data to be trained, so people's privacy is at risk if the data is misused or stolen.

questions.title: Virtual and augmented reality
questions.text: Augmented reality and virtual reality technologies are gaining popularity.

parts.title: VR vs AR
parts.text: Explain the difference between virtual and augmented reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: A virtual reality replaces your vision, augmented reality adds to it (1). VR completely covers and replaces your field of vision; AR apps show digital objects on top of the real world seen through a screen / glasses (1)

points.criterion: AR adds to the real view

scheme.model_answer: Virtual reality completely replaces what the user sees with a computer-generated world, whereas augmented reality adds digital objects to the user's view of the real world.

parts.title: VR for pilots
parts.text: Explain the purpose of virtual reality in training pilots.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Pilots practise flying / emergencies in a realistic simulated cockpit (1)
- without danger to people or aircraft / cheaper than real flights / can repeat situations (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pilots can practise dangerous situations, such as engine failure, in a realistic virtual cockpit, without risking real lives or aircraft.

parts.title: AR in a museum
parts.text: Explain how a museum could use augmented reality to improve visitors' experience.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Visitors point a phone / tablet / glasses at an exhibit and see extra information / 3D reconstructions / animations over it (1)
- making the visit more interactive / easier to understand / shows how objects looked originally (1)

points.criterion: Digital content over the real exhibit

scheme.model_answer: Visitors point their phone at a dinosaur skeleton and see it covered with muscles and skin and moving, which makes the exhibit more interesting and easier to understand.

parts.title: VR equipment
parts.text: State **one** item of hardware needed to experience virtual reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): VR headset / head-mounted display; motion controllers / data gloves; motion sensors / tracking cameras; headphones
scheme.model_answer: A VR headset.

questions.title: AI in a smart city
questions.text: A city council wants to introduce **self-driving buses** and **AI face-recognition cameras** at bus stops.

parts.title: Face recognition debate
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages for citizens of the face-recognition cameras.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantages (max 2): finds criminals / missing people; safer bus stops / deters crime; automatic fare payment / faster boarding; works 24/7
Disadvantages (max 2): privacy — every journey recorded; false matches / bias; data could be hacked or misused; expensive
Balanced answer linked to citizens for 4.
scheme.model_answer: The cameras could help police find wanted criminals and missing people, making bus stops safer, and could even let passengers pay by face. However, every citizen's journeys would be recorded, which is a loss of privacy, and the system may wrongly identify innocent people, especially if it was trained on biased data.
scheme.ai_instructions: Maximum 2 if only advantages or only disadvantages are given.

parts.title: Self-driving buses
parts.text: Identify **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of the self-driving buses.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): fewer accidents caused by tired / distracted drivers; can run 24/7; lower staff costs; efficient routes / less fuel
Disadvantage (1): bus drivers lose their jobs; unclear responsibility in an accident; may fail in unusual situations / bad weather; hacking risk; expensive
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: the buses can run all night without a driver getting tired. Disadvantage: bus drivers would lose their jobs.

parts.title: Why deep learning
parts.text: Face recognition usually uses **deep learning**. State **one** reason why.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): images are complex / unstructured data; deep neural networks find the features automatically; very large amounts of image data are available; higher accuracy for image recognition
scheme.model_answer: Faces are complex images, and deep neural networks can learn the important features of a face automatically from very large numbers of photos.

summary: What artificial intelligence is, how AI, machine learning and deep learning differ, where AI is used, its advantages and disadvantages for society, and the purpose of virtual and augmented reality.

blocks.content: The ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need **human intelligence** — such as **recognising images and speech, understanding language, making decisions, solving problems and learning from experience**.

items.title: Narrow (weak) AI
items.content: Designed for **one specific task**, and often better than humans at it: a chess program, face unlock on a phone, a spam filter, a voice assistant, a self-driving car's vision system. **All AI in use today is narrow AI.**

items.title: General (strong) AI
items.content: A hypothetical system with **human-level intelligence across all tasks** — it could learn anything a person can. It **does not exist yet**.

blocks.title: Rule-based AI vs learning AI
blocks.content: Early AI followed **rules written by programmers** (e.g. expert systems: *IF temperature > 38 AND cough THEN flu*). Modern AI mostly **learns the rules itself from data** — this is **machine learning**.

theory.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning

blocks.caption: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning

blocks.content: A branch of AI in which a computer **learns from data** (examples) to find **patterns** and make **predictions or decisions**, and **improves with experience**, **without being explicitly programmed** with the rules.

A branch of machine learning that uses **artificial neural networks with many hidden layers** ("deep" networks) to learn **complex features automatically** from very large amounts of **unstructured data** such as images, sound and text.

blocks.title: Three ways a machine can learn
rows: Thousands of e-mails labelled *spam / not spam* → the model learns to classify new e-mails
A shop groups its customers by buying habits
Learns by **trial and error**, receiving **rewards** or penalties
A program learns to play a game or a robot learns to walk

blocks.caption: A neural network: input layer, hidden layers, output layer

blocks.title: How a neural network learns (training)
items: Each connection between neurons has a **weight** (how important it is).
Training data (e.g. labelled photos) is passed through the network, which makes a **prediction**.
The prediction is compared with the correct answer; the **error** is calculated.
The weights are **adjusted** to reduce the error (back-propagation).
This is repeated thousands of times until the network is accurate. With **many hidden layers**, it is **deep learning**.

blocks.title: Try it: TensorFlow Playground
blocks.content: On **playground.tensorflow.org** you can build a small neural network in the browser, add hidden layers and neurons, and watch it learn to separate coloured dots. More hidden layers = a "deeper" network that can learn more complex patterns.

blocks.title: AI vs machine learning vs deep learning
rows: The **broad field**: machines that act intelligently
A **subset of AI**: learning from data
A **subset of ML**: learning with deep neural networks
Experts may write all the rules
Humans often choose the **features** to use (feature engineering)
Little feature engineering — the network finds features itself
Rule-based systems are easy to explain
Chess program, expert system, route planner
Spam filter, price prediction, film recommendations
Face recognition, voice assistants, self-driving cars, ChatGPT-style language models

blocks.content: **Every** deep-learning system is machine learning, and **every** machine-learning system is AI — but **not** the other way round. An expert system with hand-written rules is AI but **not** machine learning.

blocks.title: AI in different areas
rows: Diagnosing diseases from X-rays and MRI scans; predicting patient risk; drug discovery; robot-assisted surgery
Self-driving cars; traffic-light control; route planning and traffic prediction; autopilot
Adaptive learning platforms that adjust tasks to each student; automatic marking; AI tutors and chatbots
Fraud detection on bank cards; credit scoring; algorithmic trading; chatbots in banking apps
Robots on production lines; predicting machine failures (predictive maintenance); quality control with cameras
Product and film recommendations; personalised advertising; game characters that react to the player
Face recognition at airports; spotting unusual network activity; spam and malware filters
Voice assistants; machine translation; photo enhancement; smart home devices
Drones that detect crop disease; weather and climate prediction

theory.title: Advantages and disadvantages of AI for society

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- **Works 24/7** without tiredness, and **faster** than humans on many tasks.
- **Fewer human errors** — consistent decisions (e.g. detecting tumours on scans that a tired doctor might miss).
- Can do **dangerous, dirty or repetitive** jobs (bomb disposal, mining, space exploration, assembly lines).
- **Analyses huge amounts of data** to find patterns humans cannot see (fraud, disease outbreaks, climate).
- **Personalised services** — learning at your own pace, recommendations, health advice.
- Helps people with **disabilities** (speech-to-text, image description for blind users).
- Creates **new jobs** (AI engineers, data scientists) and economic growth.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- **Job losses** — routine jobs (drivers, cashiers, call-centre staff, factory workers) can be automated.
- **Bias and unfairness** — an AI trained on biased data makes biased decisions (e.g. in hiring or loans).
- **Privacy** — AI needs large amounts of **personal data**; mass surveillance with face recognition.
- **Lack of transparency** — deep learning is a "black box"; it is hard to explain decisions.
- **Accountability** — who is responsible if a self-driving car causes an accident?
- **Misuse** — deepfakes, fake news, cyber-attacks, autonomous weapons.
- **High cost** to develop, and large **energy** use for training.
- **Over-reliance** — people may lose skills or trust AI even when it is wrong; AI has no common sense or empathy.

blocks.title: Advantage + explanation (exam style)
blocks.content:
**Q: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using AI in hospitals. [2]**
Advantage: AI can analyse scans **quickly and accurately**, so diseases are diagnosed **earlier** (1).
Disadvantage: if the AI makes a wrong diagnosis it is **unclear who is responsible** / patients' **personal data** must be shared to train it (1).

theory.title: The purpose of virtual and augmented reality

blocks.content: A **computer-generated 3D environment** that **completely replaces** the user's view of the real world. The user wears a **headset** that tracks head movements and often uses **hand controllers**, so they feel **present (immersed)** in the virtual world and can interact with it. Example: Meta Quest, PlayStation VR.

Technology that **adds computer-generated information** (images, text, 3D objects, sound) **on top of the user's view of the real world**, in real time, using a phone/tablet camera or AR glasses. The real world is still seen. Examples: Pokémon GO, Google Lens translation, IKEA Place furniture app, Snapchat filters.

blocks.title: Purposes of VR and AR
rows: Pilots in flight simulators; surgeons practise operations; virtual school trips to space or history
Pointing a tablet at a textbook shows a 3D heart beating; labelled star maps
Therapy for phobias; pain distraction; rehabilitation exercises
Showing veins or organs over the patient's body during surgery
Walking through a building or car design before it is built
Repair instructions shown over a real machine
Seeing how furniture or clothes look in your room / on you
Virtual tours of museums and cities
Arrows on the street view; information about a building you look at

blocks.title: VR vs AR
rows: Limited; risk of bumping into things

blocks.title: More in Grade 12
blocks.content: VR and AR are studied in more detail in the Grade 12 topic **Virtual and augmented reality**.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Identify two differences between machine learning and deep learning. [2]**
Deep learning uses **neural networks with many layers**, whereas machine learning can use simpler models (1). Deep learning needs **much more data and computing power** than other machine-learning methods / finds the **features automatically**, whereas in ML humans often choose the features (1).

**Q: State the difference between artificial intelligence and machine learning. [1]**
AI is the **broad field** of making machines behave intelligently; ML is a **subset of AI** in which the machine **learns from data** instead of following programmed rules.

**Q: Identify two disadvantages of using AI in society. [2]**
**Job losses** as routine work is automated (1); **biased decisions** if the AI is trained on biased data (1).

**Q: Explain the purpose of augmented reality in education. [2]**
AR **adds digital 3D models and information to the real view** (1), so students can see and interact with things that are hard to imagine, e.g. a 3D model of the solar system on their desk (1).

- Treating AI, ML and DL as three **separate** things — they are **nested**: DL ⊂ ML ⊂ AI.
- Saying machine learning "is programmed with all the rules" — it **learns the rules from data**.
- Writing "AI will take all jobs" without explaining — say **which** jobs and **why** (routine, repetitive tasks).
- Mixing up VR (**replaces** the real world) and AR (**adds to** the real world).
- Giving a disadvantage that is really the opposite of an advantage already given.
